header: IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD
body: SHAHRUKH ARJUMAND, J.- Through these two jail appeals, the appellants, namely Mushtaq Khan and Daud Khan, have called in question the judgment dated 30.09.2024 (“impugned judgment”), passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge-IV, Islamabad (East) (“trial Court”), in Sessions Case No.78, arising out of FIR No.392/2012 dated 11.08.2012, registered at Police Station Shahzad Town, Islamabad, under Sections 302, 459, 148 and 149 of the Pakistan Penal Code, 1860 (“PPC”). Since both appeals arise out of the same occurrence, FIR and impugned judgment, and involve common questions of law and fact, they are being decided through this common judgment.
Appellants by : M/s Hafiz Muhammad Anees Usman, M.
Kashif Tabbassum and Adeel Ahmed Kundi, Advocates.
Respondents by : Mr. Yasir Latif, Advocate.
Mr. Waqas Haral, DDPP.
Mr. Rasheed Ahmed, SI, P.S Shahzad Town, Islamabad.

Date of Hearing : 05.10.2026 Page - 2 2. Briefly, the prosecution case, as reflected in the FIR, is that on 11.08.2012, at approximately 02:00 a.m., six armed persons, namely Ishfaq, Mushtaq Khan, Ishaq, Manan, Daud Khan and Bashir, allegedly entered the house of complainant [Taj Ud Din] (deceased) after scaling its boundary wall. It was alleged that the accused persons, armed with pistols, gathered the inmates of the house in a room and opened fire upon them. Accused Ishaq and Manan were alleged to have fired at Israr, whereas the present appellants, Mushtaq Khan and Daud Khan, were attributed firing at Waqar Younas. Accused Ishfaq and Bashir were alleged to have fired at the complainant and his wife, Zakia Bibi. Waqar Younas subsequently succumbed to his injuries on 19.08.2012. The alleged motive was resentment arising from the marriage of Israr with Mst. Nayab, which was reportedly opposed by certain members of the accused party.

3. Upon registration of the FIR, investigation commenced. The investigating agency inspected the place of occurrence, prepared the site plan, secured eight empties of 30-bore pistol and blood-stained cotton, collected medical evidence and recorded statements of witnesses. Upon the death of Waqar Younas, Section 302, PPC was added. The present appellants were subsequently declared absconders and were arrested in 2021. Following their arrest, supplementary investigation was conducted, including the alleged pointation of the place of occurrence.

4. The prosecution examined fourteen witnesses. The material evidence consisted principally of the statements of PW-7 Israr alias Siyar and PW-9 Zakia Bibi, the medical evidence of PW-3 Dr. Farrukh Kamal, the statements of the investigating officers, PW-12 Inspector Muhammad Hanif and PW-14 Inspector Aashiq Shah, and the evidence of PW-13 Muhammad Akhtar concerning the alleged pointation. The prosecution also relied upon the statement of deceased complainant Taj Ud Din recorded under Section 512, Cr.P.C., recovery memos, forensic material and other documentary evidence.

Page - 3 5. After recording the statements of the appellants under Section 342, Cr.P.C., and hearing the parties, the learned trial Court convicted both appellants under Section 302(b), PPC, and sentenced each of them to imprisonment for life, with fine of Rs.50,000/- and compensation of Rs.500,000/- payable to the legal heirs of the deceased. They were further convicted under Section 459, PPC and sentenced to imprisonment for life with fine of Rs.50,000/- each, and under Section 148, PPC to three years' imprisonment with fine of Rs.10,000/- each. The substantive sentences were ordered to run concurrently, with benefit of Section 382-B, Cr.P.C. Hence, these appeals.

Arguments of learned counsel for the appellants 6. Mr. Hafiz Muhammad Anees Usman, Advocate, learned counsel for the appellant in Jail Appeal No.360 of 2024, and Mr. Muhammad Kashif Tabassum, Advocate, learned counsel for the appellant in Jail Appeal No.359 of 2024, contend that the impugned judgment is the result of misreading and non-reading of material evidence. Learned counsel argue that the prosecution case substantially rests upon the statements of PW-7 Israr and PW-9 Zakia Bibi, whose testimony contains material improvements and inconsistencies regarding the identification of the accused, availability of illumination, manner of occurrence and attribution of individual firearm shots. They submit that the occurrence allegedly took place at 02:00 a.m., when several armed persons were firing inside a room, and that the learned trial Court failed to assess whether the witnesses had a reliable opportunity to identify the assailants and distinguish the individual acts attributed to them.

7. Learned counsel further submit that the record contains earlier judicial statements of prosecution witnesses and compromise proceedings involving co-accused, including the orders dated 26.05.2018 and 22.10.2019, which were not appropriately evaluated by the learned trial Court. They contend that PW-9 Zakia Bibi had earlier made a statement Page - 4 inconsistent with her subsequent testimony, whereas the explanation subsequently offered for that statement was not independently established. Learned counsel also refer to the earlier sworn statement of Muhammad Israr Khan recorded on 07.11.2013, the compromise affidavits and the effect of the previous proceedings upon the credibility of the prosecution witnesses.

8. Learned counsel further argue that no crime weapon was recovered from either appellant; the eight empties allegedly recovered from the place of occurrence were never forensically connected with either of them; and the blood-stained cotton, dispatched to the forensic laboratory after a considerable interval, did not establish the identity of any assailant. They further submit that the initial investigating officer admittedly failed to obtain the call-data records despite directions from his superior officer, whereas the subsequent investigation culminated merely in the alleged pointation of a place already known to the police. It is contended that the learned trial Court erroneously treated abscondence, medical evidence, recoveries and pointation as sufficient corroboration of an otherwise doubtful ocular account.

Arguments on behalf of the State 9. Conversely, learned counsel for respondent/complainant and the learned State counsel support the impugned judgment and submit that PW- 7 and PW-9 were natural witnesses of an occurrence committed inside their own residence. Their relationship with the deceased does not render their testimony unreliable. It is argued that the occurrence was promptly reported, the medical evidence corroborates the ocular account, and the appellants' prolonged abscondence constitutes an additional incriminating circumstance. Learned counsels further submits that the compromise with other co-accused does not confer any benefit upon the present appellants, particularly when the prosecution witnesses specifically attributed firing at the deceased to them. Dismissal of both appeals is accordingly sought. Page - 5 Appreciation of evidence and findings 10. I have heard learned counsel for the parties and examined the available record with their assistance. The principal question requiring determination is whether the prosecution has established beyond reasonable doubt that the present appellants participated in the occurrence and committed the offences for which they have been convicted. There is a material distinction between proof that a homicidal occurrence took place and proof that particular accused persons were responsible for it. The former, however firmly established, cannot dispense with the requirement of proving the latter.

11. It is equally necessary to clarify that the prosecution is not required to establish its case through a particular number of witnesses or through forensic evidence in every case. A conviction may lawfully rest upon trustworthy ocular testimony, even where the witnesses are related to the deceased and no crime weapon has been recovered. However, where the reliability of such testimony is affected by material contradictions, inconsistent judicial statements or doubtful circumstances of identification, the Court must examine the evidence with particular care. Neither the seriousness of the offence nor the absence of an alternative defence version can relieve the prosecution of its burden.

Earlier sworn testimony and the effect of subsequent compromise proceedings 12. A material aspect which has not received adequate consideration in the impugned judgment is the earlier judicial history of the prosecution case. The record furnished before this Court includes the statement of Muhammad Israr Khan recorded on oath on 07.11.2013 in the proceedings titled The State v. Ishaque etc. In that statement, Israr narrated that six armed persons entered the house, assembled the inmates and tied their hands. He attributed firing at himself to Ishaque (since died) and Manan, Page - 6 firing at Waqar Younas to Mushtaq Khan and Daud Khan, and firing at his parents to Bashir and Ishfaq.

13. The significance of this earlier statement is twofold. Firstly, it confirms that the prosecution had, from an earlier stage, attributed a specific role to each accused. It would therefore be incorrect to treat the mere attribution of firing to the present appellants as an improvement introduced for the first time in their subsequent trial. Secondly, the earlier statement supplies a contemporaneous judicial version against which the later testimony must be examined. The learned trial Court was required to determine whether the subsequent assertions concerning the availability of light, the sequence of firing, the manner of confinement and the opportunity of identification were consistent with the earlier version or constituted material improvements affecting credibility.

14. The record further reveals that proceedings against certain coaccused were disposed of following compromise. Co-accused Bashir Khan was acquitted by order dated 26.05.2018 on the basis of compromise, whereas co-accused Ishfaq Ahmed was acquitted through order dated 22.10.2019 passed under Sections 265-K and 345, Cr.P.C. In the latter order, the Court recorded that the complainant and injured witnesses had entered into a compromise and had not supported the prosecution to the extent of the accused then facing trial. The order also recorded that the witnesses had been declared hostile and cross-examined by the prosecution, but no sufficient incriminating material emerged to justify continuation of those proceedings.

15. The legal significance of the aforesaid orders requires careful distinction. The acquittal of Bashir Khan or Ishfaq Ahmed on compromise cannot, by itself, be treated as a judicial determination that the original occurrence was fabricated or that the present appellants were innocent. Nor can the acquittal of one accused under Section 265-K, Cr.P.C., be mechanically extended to another accused against whom a distinct role has Page - 7 been attributed. Each accused is entitled to an individual assessment of the evidence.

Nevertheless, the earlier proceedings remain relevant to the extent that they disclose previous judicial statements of witnesses who subsequently testified in the present trial. The learned trial Court was required to examine those statements, subject to the applicable rules governing proof of previous testimony and contradictions, rather than disregard their existence merely because the earlier proceedings had ended in compromise.

16. Particularly significant is the position of PW-9 Zakia Bibi. The defence relied upon her statement dated 22.10.2019, made during the proceedings against co-accused Ishfaq Ahmed, and contended that it was materially inconsistent with her subsequent testimony. PW-9 reportedly sought to explain the earlier statement by alleging coercion. Such an explanation could not be rejected merely because it was made subsequently; equally, it could not be accepted automatically without examining the circumstances in which the earlier statement was recorded, its precise contents and any supporting material regarding the alleged coercion.

The fact that the earlier statement was recorded before a competent Court, and that the prosecution was afforded an opportunity to cross-examine the witness after she was declared hostile, made a reasoned comparison necessary. The learned trial Court was required to identify the precise inconsistency, determine whether it concerned a material fact and assess whether the explanation offered by PW-9 satisfactorily reconciled the two versions. The impugned judgment does not demonstrate an adequate examination of these questions.

17. Learned counsel has also produced affidavits concerning compromise executed in March 2018. These documents refer to the same FIR and the settlement of disputes between the parties. Their existence and Page - 8 the earlier compromise proceedings are relevant to understanding the procedural history and the changing positions of the parties. However, an affidavit produced by counsel does not become substantive proof of its contents merely by being placed before the appellate Court. Its execution, admissibility, scope and relationship to the judicial record must be established in accordance with law.

Accordingly, I do not treat the affidavits as conclusive evidence of the appellants' innocence or as an independent basis for acquittal. Their proper significance is that they reinforce the necessity of examining the earlier sworn statements and judicial orders when assessing the consistency and reliability of the prosecution witnesses. The failure to undertake that exercise constitutes a material deficiency in the appreciation of evidence.

18. The prosecution's case against the present appellants must therefore be evaluated neither by automatically disbelieving the witnesses because they previously compromised with other accused persons, nor by ignoring their earlier judicial statements altogether. The decisive question remains whether their testimony, after reconciliation of the previous versions and the surrounding circumstances, establishes the participation of Mushtaq Khan and Daud Khan beyond reasonable doubt.

Reliability of the ocular account and circumstances of identification 19. The occurrence admittedly took place at approximately 02:00 a.m. The prosecution alleged that six armed persons entered the residential premises, assembled the family members in one room, tied their hands and resorted to firing. The circumstances of the occurrence are therefore important in determining whether the witnesses could reliably identify each assailant and attribute individual acts to them.

The learned trial Court appears to have attached considerable importance to the fact that PW-7 and PW-9 were natural witnesses whose presence at their residence could not ordinarily be doubted. While their presence is a Page - 9 relevant circumstance, it is not synonymous with the reliability of every part of their testimony. A witness may genuinely have been present during an occurrence and yet be mistaken regarding the identity or individual acts of an assailant, particularly where the occurrence is sudden, violent and takes place during nighttime.

20. PW-7 introduced particulars concerning illumination, the circumstances of Ramadan, the tying of the inmates and the manner in which the assailants departed. The materiality of these particulars lies in their bearing upon the witnesses' opportunity to observe the occurrence. The scaled site plan, Ex.PC, does not identify a specific source of illumination inside the room. The omission of a light source from a site plan is not, by itself, sufficient to discredit an eyewitness. Nevertheless, where the availability of illumination assumes importance in determining the reliability of identification, and the relevant particulars are introduced or elaborated upon subsequently, the Court must determine whether they are consistent with the earlier account.

The learned trial Court did not sufficiently distinguish between ordinary discrepancies arising from lapse of time and improvements relating directly to the opportunity of identification. The latter category cannot be dismissed as minor without examining its effect upon the prosecution's case.

21. It is also significant that the witnesses attributed separate firearm roles to several assailants during an occurrence allegedly involving firing inside a confined room. The earlier statement of Israr Khan dated 07.11.2013 specifically attributed firing at Waqar Younas to Mushtaq Khan and Daud Khan. Thus, the difficulty does not arise merely from the existence of a specific attribution. It arises from whether that attribution remained reliable after considering the circumstances of observation, the later testimony, the earlier judicial proceedings and the absence of independent evidence connecting either appellant with a firearm used in the occurrence.

Page - 10 In Munir Ahmed and others v. The State and others (2019 SCMR 2006), the Hon'ble Supreme Court examined the evidentiary difficulties associated with assigning precise roles to multiple assailants during indiscriminate firing. The principle is not that such attribution is invariably unreliable, but that its credibility must be tested against the actual circumstances of the occurrence. Applying that approach, the learned trial Court was required to assess the prosecution version as a whole instead of treating the repetition of the same attribution as sufficient proof of its accuracy.

22. The alleged injuries sustained by PW-7 and PW-9 also required separate examination. If duly established, injuries sustained during the same occurrence may provide substantial assurance of a witness's presence. However, the existence of injuries does not automatically establish the correctness of identification or the truth of every allegation made by that witness. The medical evidence must be examined to determine which injuries were proved, upon whom they were inflicted and whether their nature is consistent with the particular version advanced. In the present case, the prosecution's assertion that the eyewitnesses themselves sustained injuries was not satisfactorily reconciled with the available medical material. The learned trial Court could not legitimately use the status of an injured eyewitness as an additional guarantee of truthfulness without first determining the evidentiary foundation for that status.

Medical evidence and the limits of corroboration 23. PW-3 Dr. Farrukh Kamal conducted the postmortem examination of Waqar Younas and described the firearm injuries and cause of death. His evidence supports the conclusion that the deceased sustained firearm injuries and subsequently died as a result thereof. However, medical evidence ordinarily establishes the nature, seat, extent and probable cause Page - 11 of injuries; it does not independently establish the identity of the person who inflicted them.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court has reiterated this distinction in its jurisprudence concerning the evidentiary limits of medical corroboration. The medical evidence may support the manner of an occurrence but cannot, without more, supply a missing link concerning the identity of the offender.
24. PW-9 Zakia Bibi, during cross-examination, stated:
“I was at about 10 feet away from the accused persons when they were firing. The deceased was also at about same distance.”

The postmortem evidence did not record blackening or charring around the firearm wounds. It would be unsafe to infer from this circumstance alone that firing from approximately ten feet was medically impossible. The absence of blackening or charring depends upon several factors, including the firearm, ammunition and firing distance, and no categorical conclusion can be drawn without an adequate scientific foundation.

Nevertheless, the medical evidence does not independently verify the precise distance or individual firearm roles asserted by PW-9. Its proper evidentiary value is confined to corroborating the firearm occurrence and the resulting injuries. The learned trial Court erred to the extent that it treated medical consistency as corroboration of the identity of Mushtaq Khan and Daud Khan.

25. Another circumstance concerns the treatment record of Taj Ud Din, which records a history of firearm injuries during a robbery, whereas the prosecution attributed the occurrence to a matrimonial dispute. The history recorded in a medical document is not substantive proof that a robbery actually took place, and its source must be considered. Nevertheless, the existence of a contemporaneous account referring to robbery required Page - 12 consideration, particularly where the prosecution relied upon a specific matrimonial dispute as motive.

The learned trial Court was required to determine whether this entry was merely an inaccurate or incomplete description of the occurrence or whether it reflected a material inconsistency in the prosecution narrative. In the absence of a satisfactory reconciliation, the entry remains a circumstance requiring caution, though not an independent ground for rejecting the prosecution case.

Recovery of eight empties and blood-stained cotton 26. The prosecution relied upon recovery memo Ex.PE concerning blood-stained cotton and recovery memo Ex.PF concerning eight empties of 30-bore pistol, allegedly recovered from the place of occurrence on 11.08.2012. These recoveries were treated by the learned trial Court as circumstances corroborating the prosecution case.

There is, however, a fundamental distinction between evidence corroborating the occurrence of firing and evidence identifying the persons responsible for that firing. The recovery of empties may support the allegation that shots were fired at the relevant place. Yet no weapon was recovered from either appellant, and no ballistic comparison was produced establishing that any of the recovered empties had been fired from a weapon possessed or used by Mushtaq Khan or Daud Khan.

Accordingly, the recovery of eight empties does not independently connect either appellant with the occurrence. The learned trial Court was required to identify the precise incriminating link supplied by this recovery instead of treating its mere existence as corroboration of the eyewitnesses' identification.

27. The evidence of PW-12 Inspector Muhammad Hanif is particularly relevant to the custody and transmission of the recovered material. In his Page - 13 recalled statement recorded on 19.08.2024, he deposed that on 01.11.2012 he procured a letter for sending the eight empties to the Punjab Forensic Science Agency, Lahore. According to him, Moharrir Malkhana Muhammad Afzal 1716/HC handed over the empties to Arshad Mehmood 8050/C for onward transmission. He further stated that on 08.11.2012, the Moharrir Malkhana handed over a sealed parcel of blood-stained cotton, bearing the stamp of “MH”, to Sikandar Ali 6677/LHC for onward transmission to the forensic laboratory.

The testimony establishes the investigating officer's account of the arrangements for dispatch. However, it does not, by itself, establish every intervening stage of safe custody from the date of recovery until delivery to the laboratory. That question must be assessed through the relevant malkhana entries, evidence of the custodial officials, transmission documents and laboratory receipts.

28. The blood-stained cotton was allegedly recovered on 11.08.2012 and dispatched on 08.11.2012, approximately eighty-nine days later. Similarly, the empties were recovered on 11.08.2012, whereas the evidence of PW-12 places the arrangements for their transmission on 01.11.2012. Such intervals do not automatically render the recoveries inadmissible or establish that the parcels were tampered with. Nevertheless, where the prosecution seeks to rely upon forensic material as corroborative evidence, the identity and integrity of the material submitted for examination must be satisfactorily established.

In The State through Regional Director, ANF v. Imam Bakhsh and others (2018 SCMR 2039), the Hon'ble Supreme Court emphasized the importance of an unbroken and secure chain of custody. That decision arose under the special narcotics regime and cannot be mechanically applied to a murder prosecution. The general evidentiary concern regarding preservation and identity of forensic material, however, remains relevant. Page - 14 29. Even if the prosecution is given the benefit of assuming that the recovered material remained safely preserved and was transmitted intact, the result does not materially strengthen the case concerning the appellants' identity. The PFSA report, Ex.PY, concerning the cotton reflects a presumptive indication of human blood. It does not identify the source of that blood or connect the material with either appellant.

Likewise, the empties were not connected through a recovered firearm or ballistic comparison with Mushtaq Khan or Daud Khan. Consequently, the deficiencies in custody and transmission are not the sole basis for rejecting the forensic evidence. More fundamentally, the forensic evidence, even if accepted at its highest value, does not establish the participation of the appellants.
The learned trial Court failed to give adequate consideration to this distinction.

Admissions of PW-12 regarding incomplete investigation 30. During cross-examination, PW-12 Inspector Muhammad Hanif made an important admission concerning the collection of call-data records. He stated:

“It is correct that on 27.03.2013 SDPO/DSP Investigation directed me to obtain CDR of the accused persons. I could not collect the said CDR because I was transferred after 5/6 days of the said direction.”
He denied the suggestion that the call-data records had been collected but withheld because the locations of the accused did not support the prosecution case.

31. The admission establishes that the superior investigating officer had directed collection of potentially relevant objective evidence, but that evidence was not collected by PW-12. The defence suggestion that the Page - 15 records were deliberately suppressed cannot be accepted as proved, since the witness expressly denied it and no independent material establishing suppression has been identified.

Nevertheless, the admitted failure to collect the records is relevant. Where the occurrence took place at night and the identity and participation of the accused are disputed, objective evidence concerning their movements could have assisted the investigation. The prosecution cannot be presumed to have suppressed evidence merely because it was not collected; equally, the Court cannot treat an investigation as complete in every material respect when the investigating officer himself acknowledged that a direction to obtain relevant evidence remained unimplemented.

32. PW-12 also acknowledged that he had not placed on the record the Roznamcha entries concerning his arrival and departure from the police station in connection with his visits to the native village of the accused persons. He denied that he had never visited the village.

The absence of those entries does not conclusively establish that the investigating officer failed to visit the relevant place. It does, however, deprive the prosecution of documentary support for that part of the investigation. Considered alongside the admitted failure to collect call-data records, the omission demonstrates that certain potentially verifiable aspects of the investigation were left without objective corroboration. The learned trial Court was required to examine these admissions in their proper context rather than treat the investigation as wholly satisfactory merely because the investigating officer supported the prosecution narrative.

Alleged pointation and the evidence of PW-13 and PW-14 33. The prosecution further relied upon the alleged pointation of the place of occurrence on 16.09.2021, approximately nine years after the Page - 16 incident. PW-13 Muhammad Akhtar 4412/HC stated that both appellants disclosed their ability to identify the place of occurrence and were taken there in vehicle No. GAC-618, accompanied by the investigating officer and other police officials. According to him, the appellants identified the place and a pointation memo was prepared.

During cross-examination, PW-13 admitted that both appellants were taken in the same vehicle, that he could not state the number of rooms in the house, and that the police party spent approximately thirty to thirty-five minutes at the spot. He further stated that Israr was present there and that no private person was present outside the house when the police party arrived.

34. PW-14 Inspector Aashiq Shah supplied further particulars of the alleged exercise. He stated that on 16.09.2021 the appellants were taken to the house of the complainant in Burma Town. According to him, Mushtaq Khan knocked at the door, which was opened by Israr, and thereafter Mushtaq Khan and Daud Khan separately identified the same room as the place of occurrence. He prepared the pointation memo, Ex.PX. PW-14 further stated that the appellants disclosed having thrown away their weapons after the occurrence, but no weapon was recovered. During cross-examination, he admitted:
“It is correct that no witness tell me about the fact regarding throwing the weapon neither I recorded the statement regarding that fact.”

35. The significance of this admission is that the allegation regarding disposal of the weapons remained unsupported by any subsequent discovery or independent evidence. No weapon was recovered, no place of concealment was discovered, and no material object was produced as a result of the alleged disclosure.

Page - 17 More importantly, the house and the room in which the occurrence allegedly took place had been known to the police since 2012. The alleged pointation in 2021 therefore did not disclose any previously unknown fact concerning the place of occurrence.

In Hayatullah v. The State (2018 SCMR 2092), the Hon'ble Supreme Court discussed the evidentiary limitations of pointing out a place already known to the investigating agency in the context of Article 40 of the Qanun-e- Shahadat Order, 1984.

36. The learned trial Court was required to distinguish between a discovery of a new incriminating fact and a subsequent identification of a place already within the knowledge of the police. In the present case, the pointation was made at the complainant's own house, in the presence of Israr, and resulted in no recovery or discovery. It cannot therefore be regarded as independent corroboration of the appellants' participation. The discrepancies concerning the particulars of the room or the precise sequence of the alleged pointation are not, by themselves, decisive. The fundamental deficiency is that the exercise produced no new incriminating evidence capable of linking either appellant with the offence. Statement of deceased complainant under Section 512, Cr.P.C.

37. The prosecution also relied upon the statement of deceased complainant Taj Ud Din recorded under Section 512, Cr.P.C., during the abscondence of the appellants. The law permits preservation and subsequent use of such evidence where the statutory conditions are satisfied. It would therefore be legally incorrect to exclude the statement merely because it was recorded in the appellants' absence. In Arbab Tasleem v. The State (PLD 2010 SC 642), the Hon'ble Supreme Court explained that evidence recorded under Section 512, Cr.P.C., may be admissible in the circumstances prescribed by law, but its evidentiary Page - 18 weight must be assessed with regard to its intrinsic reliability and supporting circumstances.

38. In the present case, Taj Ud Din had died before the appellants were put to trial. His earlier deposition was therefore capable of being considered, subject to satisfaction of the statutory requirements. The learned trial Court, however, was still required to evaluate its reliability, compare it with the surviving eyewitness testimony and examine whether any material inconsistency affected the prosecution's case. The fact that the complainant's deposition was admissible did not render it conclusive. Equally, the appellants' inability to cross-examine him after his death did not, by itself, render the deposition worthless. Its probative value depended upon the substance of the statement and the degree to which it was supported by other trustworthy evidence.

39. The trial Court appears to have relied upon the complainant's earlier account as supporting the later testimony of PW-7 and PW-9 without adequately addressing the material questions arising from the subsequent judicial proceedings and the witnesses' inconsistent positions. Repetition of an allegation in several statements does not necessarily constitute independent corroboration where the reliability of the underlying account itself requires examination.

The statement of Taj Ud Din, therefore, had to be evaluated as part of the entire evidentiary record. It could not be treated as a substitute for the Court's independent assessment of the reliability of the surviving eyewitnesses.

Effect of acquittal of co-accused and the principle of consistency Page - 19 40. Learned counsel for the appellants has emphasized that co-accused Bashir Khan and Ishfaq Ahmed were acquitted in earlier proceedings arising from the same FIR. The orders dated 26.05.2018 and 22.10.2019 have already been discussed. The distinction between acquittal following compromise and acquittal upon a finding that the prosecution evidence is unreliable is legally significant.

The present appellants cannot claim acquittal merely because other accused persons obtained acquittal on compromise. The doctrine of consistency does not require identical treatment of accused persons whose cases were disposed of on different legal grounds. Nor can the statements made by the complainant party during compromise proceedings automatically be treated as a retraction of every allegation against all accused persons.

41. Nevertheless, the earlier proceedings cannot be regarded as wholly irrelevant. The same occurrence, the same complainant family and substantially the same attribution of roles formed the basis of the prosecution case. The subsequent judicial statements of the witnesses were therefore material to the assessment of their credibility, provided those statements were properly proved and used in accordance with the applicable rules of evidence.

The learned trial Court was required to consider whether the witnesses' earlier positions affected the reliability of their later testimony and whether any material inconsistency had been satisfactorily explained. The deficiency in the impugned judgment lies not in its failure to extend the compromise automatically to the appellants, but in its failure to undertake a sufficiently reasoned examination of the earlier judicial record.

42. In Tariq v. The State (2017 SCMR 1672), Maqsood Alam v. The State and others (2024 SCMR 156) and Shaukat Hussain v. The State (2024 SCMR 929), the Hon'ble Supreme Court considered the importance of Page - 20 consistent and cautious appreciation of prosecution evidence where the credibility of an ocular account had been materially affected. Those authorities do not establish that every acquittal of a co-accused entitles the remaining accused to the same result. Their relevance is that, where a prosecution account has become doubtful in material particulars, the Court must carefully examine whether the evidence against the accused whose conviction is under consideration remains independently trustworthy.

In the present case, the prosecution attributed specific firing at Waqar Younas to Mushtaq Khan and Daud Khan. That attribution has to be judged on its own merits. The earlier compromise orders are not an independent ground for acquittal; they form part of the broader assessment of the witnesses' consistency and reliability.

Non-examination of Mst. Nayab and failure to independently establish the alleged motive 43. Another material aspect of the prosecution case, which escaped adequate consideration by the learned trial Court, is the non-examination of Mst. Nayab, whose marriage with PW-7 Israr allegedly constituted the very foundation of the motive attributed to the accused persons. According to the prosecution, accused Ishaq had desired to marry Mst. Nayab, but her marriage was contracted with Israr, son of the complainant, which allegedly caused resentment among the accused persons and ultimately led to the occurrence. Thus, Mst. Nayab was not merely a person incidentally mentioned in the prosecution narrative; rather, she was directly connected with the matrimonial dispute upon which the prosecution sought to establish motive.

44. Despite her central position in the alleged matrimonial dispute, Mst. Nayab was not produced in the witness box. She could potentially have furnished direct evidence regarding the circumstances surrounding her Page - 21 marriage, whether any proposal had previously been made by accused Ishaq, whether she or her family had received threats or objections, and whether any hostility had developed between the parties on account of her marriage with Israr. Such evidence would have been particularly relevant because the prosecution attributed the origin of the occurrence to resentment over the said marriage. However, no explanation appears on the available record as to why she was not examined, nor was any independent evidence produced to satisfactorily establish the alleged resentment of the present appellants.

45. It is pertinent to observe that the non-examination of a particular witness does not invariably render the prosecution case doubtful. Under Article 17 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, read with the settled principles governing appreciation of evidence, the prosecution is not required to examine every person who may possess some knowledge of the occurrence. Nevertheless, where a witness is naturally placed to explain a material circumstance relied upon by the prosecution, and such circumstance remains otherwise unsubstantiated, the withholding of that witness without satisfactory explanation assumes significance. Article 129(g) of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, permits the Court, in appropriate circumstances, to draw an adverse inference where evidence which could have been produced is withheld. Such inference is not automatic and must depend upon the materiality and availability of the witness and the surrounding circumstances.

46. The prosecution's failure to examine Mst. Nayab is particularly relevant when considered in conjunction with the nature of the motive alleged. The alleged resentment was principally attributed to co-accused Ishaq, who reportedly wished to marry her. No convincing independent evidence was produced to establish that Mushtaq Khan and Daud Khan themselves had opposed the marriage, threatened Israr or Mst. Nayab, or otherwise demonstrated hostility towards Waqar Younas on account of the matrimonial dispute. The mere fact that the appellants were related to the Page - 22 other accused persons could not, without supporting evidence, justify an inference that they necessarily shared the alleged resentment or possessed a common intention or object to commit the offences in question.

47. The learned trial Court appears to have accepted the alleged motive substantially on the basis of the statements of PW-7 Israr and PW-9 Zakia Bibi, without adequately examining whether the underlying matrimonial dispute had been independently established or whether the alleged hostility could reasonably be attributed to the present appellants. More importantly, the absence of an explanation from the appellants regarding the alleged motive could not be treated as proof of its existence. The burden remained throughout upon the prosecution, and no weakness in the defence could relieve it of that obligation.

48. It is equally important to distinguish the failure to prove motive from the failure to prove participation. Motive is not an indispensable ingredient of the offence of murder where the prosecution produces otherwise trustworthy and confidence-inspiring direct evidence. Conversely, even a proved motive cannot substitute for reliable evidence identifying the actual perpetrators. In the present case, where the ocular account is already affected by material questions concerning identification, earlier inconsistent judicial statements and the circumstances of the nighttime occurrence, the absence of independent evidence regarding the alleged matrimonial dispute further deprives the prosecution of a potentially corroborative circumstance. The non-examination of Mst. Nayab, therefore, is not treated as an independent ground for acquittal, but constitutes an additional factor which must be considered in the cumulative assessment of the prosecution evidence.

Abscondence of accused and its effect upon the prosecution case 49. The learned trial Court also attached significance to the appellants' prolonged abscondence. The record indicates that they were not arrested Page - 23 until 2021, approximately nine years after the occurrence. Their absence from the proceedings was undoubtedly a circumstance which the Court was entitled to consider.

However, abscondence does not constitute substantive proof of the commission of an offence. In Rafaqat Ali alias Foji v. The State and others (2024 SCMR 1579), the Hon'ble Supreme Court reiterated that mere abscondence cannot independently form the basis of conviction and may be considered only in conjunction with reliable substantive evidence.

50. The appellants' alleged abscondence could not therefore be employed to overcome material doubts concerning their identification and participation. Even assuming that the prosecution established deliberate evasion of the process of law, the circumstance could lend support only to an otherwise trustworthy prosecution case. It could not supply the missing connection between the appellants and the commission of the offence. The learned trial Court appears to have accorded this circumstance greater weight than it could legally bear, particularly when the other material relied upon as corroboration did not independently identify either appellant as an assailant.

Separate consideration of the offences under Sections 459 and 148, PPC 51. The learned trial Court also convicted the appellants under Sections 459 and 148, PPC. These convictions required separate consideration of the statutory ingredients of the respective offences.

As regards Section 459, PPC, the prosecution was required to establish the relevant house-trespass or house-breaking and the causing of hurt or grievous hurt in the course of that offence. The occurrence of firing and injuries inside the residential premises may support the prosecution's account of the incident. However, the appellants' individual participation in Page - 24 the alleged unlawful entry and associated violence remained dependent upon the reliability of the same disputed ocular evidence.

52. Similarly, the conviction under Section 148, PPC required proof that the appellants were members of an unlawful assembly and participated in rioting while armed with deadly weapons. The prosecution's allegation that several persons entered the premises armed with pistols was not, by itself, sufficient to establish the membership and participation of each appellant unless their identity and presence were proved through reliable evidence. The learned trial Court was therefore required to examine whether the evidence independently satisfied the ingredients of these offences. Once reasonable doubt arose concerning the appellants' identification and participation in the alleged occurrence, the convictions under Sections 459 and 148, PPC could not be sustained merely by reference to the fact that the occurrence itself involved unlawful entry and firearm violence. Deficiencies in the impugned judgment 53. Upon examining the impugned judgment in the light of the prosecution evidence, I find that the learned trial Court did not sufficiently distinguish between evidence proving the occurrence and evidence proving the participation of the present appellants. The principal deficiencies in its appreciation of evidence may be summarized as follows:

First, the learned trial Court placed substantial reliance upon the consistency of the ocular account without adequately reconciling the earlier sworn testimony, subsequent judicial statements and material improvements relating to identification and the circumstances of the nighttime occurrence.

Secondly, the earlier compromise proceedings involving co-accused, particularly the judicial order dated 22.10.2019 and the position taken by the prosecution witnesses in those proceedings, were not examined with sufficient care for their possible bearing upon credibility. Page - 25 Thirdly, the medical evidence was treated as corroborative of the prosecution case without adequately distinguishing its value in establishing firearm injuries from its inability to identify the particular assailants. Fourthly, the recovery of eight empties and blood-stained cotton was accorded corroborative value against the appellants notwithstanding the absence of any recovered crime weapon, ballistic connection or forensic identification linking either appellant with the recovered material. Fifthly, the admissions of PW-12 concerning the uncollected call-data records and the absence of supporting Roznamcha entries were not sufficiently considered in assessing the completeness and reliability of the investigation.
Sixthly, the alleged pointation of a place already known to the investigating agency was treated as incriminating notwithstanding the absence of any discovery or recovery of a weapon.

Lastly, the prolonged abscondence of the appellants was relied upon without adequately recognizing that such conduct cannot substitute for proof of their participation through trustworthy substantive evidence.

54. None of the aforesaid deficiencies should be considered in isolation or exaggerated beyond its legitimate evidentiary significance. The failure to recover a weapon is not invariably fatal. Delay in transmitting forensic material does not automatically establish tampering. An omission from a site plan does not necessarily discredit an eyewitness. The compromise of a co-accused does not entitle another accused to acquittal. Likewise, an investigation may contain defects without necessarily undermining an otherwise trustworthy prosecution case.

The question is whether, after taking account of all these circumstances and evaluating the prosecution evidence as a whole, the Court can safely conclude that the appellants' guilt has been established beyond reasonable doubt.

Cumulative assessment of prosecution evidence 55. Having examined the prosecution evidence in its entirety, I find that the prosecution has established the occurrence of firearm injuries and the subsequent death of Waqar Younas. The medical evidence, recovery of Page - 26 empties and presence of blood-stained material support the occurrence of a violent incident at the relevant place. However, the existence of that occurrence does not automatically establish that the present appellants were responsible for it.

The prosecution's case concerning the participation of Mushtaq Khan and Daud Khan rests substantially upon the ocular account of PW-7 and PW-9, read with the earlier statement of deceased complainant Taj Ud Din. The reliability of that account required careful assessment in the light of the nighttime circumstances, the alleged firing by several armed persons, the particulars concerning illumination, the earlier judicial statements and the subsequent compromise proceedings.

56. The learned trial Court appears to have proceeded upon the premise that the witnesses' presence in the house, their relationship with the deceased and the consistency of the attributed firearm roles were sufficient to establish the appellants' guilt. Such an approach did not adequately address the material questions concerning the witnesses' opportunity of observation and the effect of their previous judicial statements. The subsequent investigative material did not satisfactorily resolve those questions. No crime weapon was recovered from either appellant. The eight empties were not connected with them through ballistic examination. The blood-stained cotton did not establish the identity of any assailant. The alleged pointation resulted in no discovery. The motive was not independently established against the appellants, whereas the investigating officer admitted that potentially relevant call-data records had not been collected.

57. It is necessary to emphasize that the Court is not rejecting the prosecution case merely because independent forensic corroboration is absent. Trustworthy direct evidence may itself be sufficient to sustain a conviction. The difficulty in the present case is that the ocular account, Page - 27 upon which the prosecution substantially depends, is affected by material questions of reliability which the learned trial Court did not satisfactorily resolve. The remaining evidence, although capable of supporting the occurrence, does not independently remove the doubts concerning the identity and participation of the appellants.

The evidence must therefore be assessed cumulatively, rather than by treating several circumstances which establish the occurrence as though they independently corroborate the identity of the offenders. Benefit of doubt 58. The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in Muhammad Akram v. The State (2009 SCMR 230), while reiterating the principle laid down in Tariq Pervez v. The State (1995 SCMR 1345), held that even a single circumstance creating reasonable doubt in the mind of a prudent person is sufficient to entitle an accused to its benefit as a matter of right and not of grace. The principle was also reiterated in Abdul Qadeer v. The State (2024 SCMR 1146), emphasizing that the prosecution must establish its case through its own evidence and cannot rely upon weaknesses in the defence to discharge the burden of proof.

59. The doubts arising in the present case are neither imaginary nor speculative. They arise from the prosecution record itself and concern the fundamental question whether the appellants were reliably identified as participants in the occurrence. The earlier judicial statements, subsequent compromise proceedings, material questions concerning nighttime identification, limitations of the medical and forensic evidence, absence of discovery pursuant to pointation and admitted investigative omissions collectively render the prosecution case unsafe for sustaining the convictions. The seriousness of the offence and the tragic death of Waqar Younas cannot justify lowering the standard of proof. The Court must decide the criminal responsibility of the accused upon legally admissible Page - 28 and reliable evidence, not upon the gravity of the accusation or the consequences of the occurrence.

60. In view of the foregoing discussion, I am of the considered opinion that the learned trial Court failed to appreciate the material evidence in its proper perspective and attached undue corroborative value to circumstances which did not independently establish the appellants' participation. The findings of conviction, therefore, cannot be sustained beyond reasonable doubt. The appellants are consequently entitled to the benefit of doubt.

Conclusion 61. For the reasons recorded above, Jail Appeal No.359 of 2024 filed by Mushtaq Khan and Jail Appeal No.360 of 2024 filed by Daud Khan are allowed. The impugned judgment dated 30.09.2024, passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge-IV, Islamabad (East), to the extent of the present appellants, is hereby set aside. Their convictions and sentences under Sections 302(b), 459 and 148, PPC, including the fines and compensation awarded thereunder, are set aside, and both appellants are acquitted of the charges by extending them the benefit of doubt.

62. The appellants shall be released forthwith, if not required to be detained in any other case. The Superintendent of the concerned jail shall be informed accordingly. A copy of this judgment shall be transmitted to the learned trial Court for information and compliance.
